summary: xAI's Grok Build coding agent, driven in a terminal.

auto.$comment: Grok ships the full Claude Code mode set: `grok --help` lists `--permission-mode [default, acceptEdits, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissions, plan]`. It also has `--sandbox <PROFILE>`, not used here. --trust rides this rung as well as bypass, decided deliberately (MC-2211): without it Grok skips project-level .grok hooks, so no agent-state frames arrive and the session converts to `stalled` via the runtime watchdog — an auto session that always reads as stalled is worse than useless. The trust decision is defensible HERE because auto is not the safe default: `manual` is, and it carries no trust, so a freshly cloned untrusted repo still gets no repo-committed hooks unless the user asks for autonomy.
auto.label: Auto — Grok reviews each action instead of you

bypass.$comment: --trust rides this preset, never the default launch argv: it does not just enable Multicode's own .grok/hooks agent-state reporter — it trusts EVERY project-level .grok config, including hooks committed in the repo itself, so a freshly cloned untrusted repo must not get it under the safe default. Without trust Grok skips project hooks, so no frames arrive and the session converts to the stalled phase via the runtime watchdog (there is no output-timing fallback any more); the user can grant trust in the TUI via /hooks-trust. Kept as `--always-approve` rather than switched to `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`: both exist in `grok --help` and this one is what shipped and is covered by tests, so MC-2211 adds the missing auto rung without churning a working bypass.
bypass.label: Bypass all approvals (dangerous)

promptInjection.$comment: Grok Build's interactive TUI documents no positional prompt argument (headless -p is a one-shot, not a session). The pattern (?!) never matches by design: Grok's real input-ready marker is unknown, and any guessable pattern (e.g. the brand name) matches the startup banner before the TUI accepts input — injecting there both swallows the keystrokes and cancels the timeout fallback, while a post-timeout late match would inject a second copy. Never-match makes delivery deterministic: exactly one injection, via the runtime's timeout fallback, after the TUI has had timeoutMs to become ready. If a real install confirms `grok "prompt"` works interactively (Claude Code parity), flip mode to positional-arg — config-only change.

installTargets.$comment: restartRequired NOT verified on 2026-07-29: the probe could not reach an interactive session because this machine is not signed in to Grok (the TUI sits on its browser-approval screen). Left true — a banner that over-warns is recoverable, one that under-warns is not. Verify by adding a skill directory while `grok` runs and checking its /skill picker.

agentStateSpec.$comment: Grok Build ships Claude-style lifecycle hooks (same event vocabulary; stdin payload uses camelCase field names — hookEventName / sessionId — which the shared reporter reads alongside snake_case). Discovery is per-file: project hooks are standalone JSON files under .grok/hooks/, so we own our config file outright (owned-json). Project hooks only run once the folder is trusted — see the bypass_all $comment. Grok's Notification payload types are UNVERIFIED against the awaiting-input allow-list (its docs name no notification_type values), so until confirmed live a Grok permission prompt may read as idle — the deliberate fail-safe direction (a false needs-input parks a session forever; a false idle is recoverable).

capabilities.$comment: resumeSession is intentionally false pending end-to-end verification (the MC-1464/MC-1465 discipline: an unverified resume path must not risk a lost conversation). Grok Build documents claude-style resume (-s/--session-id at launch, -r/--resume <id> on relaunch) and the resume argv above is wired for it, so once resume is verified against a real Grok Build install, flip this to true — no code change needed. sessionIdFromCaller is true because launch passes our minted --session-id.
